To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

doxorubicin treatment can have a profound transient effect on PARP activity and its expression in PBMC from patients and animals and this should be taken into account in the interpretation of PARP activity as a pharmacodynamic biomarker in clinical trials.

doxorubicin can have a profound impact on the activity and expression of PARP-1 in PBMCs, which may affect the interpretation of results from clinical trials where PAR activity is used as the pharmacodynamic endpoint for PARP inhibitors.
doxorubicin can suppress the activity of the DNA repair enzyme, PARP-1, in human peripheral blood mononucleated cells and that the effects of this drug on PARP-1 are reversible.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of DOX on PBMCs and its implication for the use of PARP activity as a biomarker for PARP inhibitors.
the effects of DOX treatment on PARP-1 activity and expression and the implications of these findings for PARP-1 inhibitor clinical trials.
the effects of DOX on PARP activity and the implications for PARP inhibition studies in clinical trials.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the PARP activity in the PBMCs of the patient was suppressed by DOX and not the PARP inhibitor.
PARP activity and PARP-1 levels should be measured in PBMCs before and after DOX treatment and not be used as a pharmacogenomic endpoint in clinical trials.
the PARP inhibitor is not effective in the clinical trial, as the patient's PBMC PARP activity has been suppressed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
DOX is an inhibitor of PARP and that PARP inhibitors should be tested against DOX to determine the effect of the drug on the PARP activity.
PARP activity is not a reliable marker of PARP-1 inhibition in clinical trials.
PARP activity and/or expression in PBMC is not a suitable pharmacodynamic marker for PARP inhibitors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of PBMCs as a surrogate tissue for PARP activity and PARP-1 mRNA expression in clinical studies should be used with caution.
PARP inhibitors should not be used in patients who have recently received chemotherapy.
the effect of chemotherapeutics should be taken into consideration when interpreting the results of PARP pharmacogenetic and pharmacodynamic studies.
